item.title: Waikiki's iconic 'Pink Palace' is getting a major makeover for its 100th birthday
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Waikiki's iconic 'Pink Palace' is getting a major makeover for its 100th birthday The Royal Hawaiian, an iconic part of Honolulu's Waikiki Beach for nearly a century and one of the world's most famous hotels, is getting an extreme makeover, just in time for its 100th birthday celebration. The hotel, also known as the "Pink Palace of the Pacific," turns 100 in February of 2027, and the renovations are on track to be fully completed in time for the big birthday. The hotel is open during the remodel, with sections shut down as part of a staged renovation. Set on a prime stretch of Waikiki Beach, The Royal Hawaiian has been attracting guests for generations. Built in 1927 in a Spanish-Moorish style, it was one of the earliest major resorts in Waikiki, following its older sister property, the Moana Surfrider, which opened in 1901. The Royal Hawaiian is part of Marriott's collection of hotels in Honolulu, which means it's bookable with Marriott Bonvoy points. The renovations are ongoing, but don't worry, there are no plans to ditch the famous pink stucco exteriors. I got to stay at this historic property late last year, and the rooms were lovely, but a refresh will be welcome. I stayed in the historic wing, the original part of the hotel, with its huge rooms and tall ceilings. There are 349 rooms and suites in the six-story wing. The remodeled rooms (pictured below) will all have custom-carved furniture, dining tables for two and new bathrooms with glass shower doors and new vanities. According to the hotel, " ... each guest room subtly nods to the golden age of travel, including styling elements reminiscent of vintage steamer trunks and elegant furnishings that evoke the curving lines of the building." For fans of the historic property, the hotel is keeping the historic wing's original wooden doors carved with the Hawaii state seal. The Mailani Tower, which opened in 1969, is getting a full renovation, with all 179 rooms (including 11 suites) totally redone. All rooms face the ocean and have a private lanai. The lobby and public areas are also getting a big makeover, with lighter fabrics and furnishings. I got to check out another new addition to the hotel: a Historic Gallery that opened late last year in partnership with Matson Archives. The hotel offers twice-weekly historic tours that take you through the new space filled with artifacts from the 1920s, including those from its grand opening gala. The hotel has announced a series of major commemorations around the anniversary, including a special Royal Hawaiian Ahaaina Luau, the opening of a time capsule and a series of parties. Tickets for the events go on sale Oct. 21. "This once-in-a-generation milestone offers an opportunity to celebrate the Pink Palace of the Pacific's extraordinary heritage, honor the cherished stories that have shaped its remarkable history, and create new memories that will inspire future generations for years to come," said Nicole Okuna, general manager and the fourth woman to lead the resort. Hopefully, TPG can check out the fully completed renovations after the grand reopening and 100th birthday party early next year. Related reading:

item.title: Southwest is changing how you earn a Companion Pass, and there's some bad news
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Southwest is changing how you earn a Companion Pass, and there's some bad news There's a lot of news today from Southwest Airlines, including new elite status tiers and qualification requirements, a first look at its forthcoming Icon Lounges, faster ways to earn Tier Qualifying Points toward elite status and more. But there's one change that really jumped out at me: The way you qualify for a Southwest Companion Pass is changing in 2027, and some points travelers aren't going to like it. For years, the Southwest Companion Pass has allowed a designated companion to fly with the passholder for just the cost of taxes and fees. It's a valuable and much-loved perk that many travelers chase year after year. But beginning in 2027, the Companion Pass will become a benefit of Southwest's newly announced top-tier Platinum status, meaning travelers will need to qualify using Tier Qualifying Points (TQPs) or qualifying flights. And that comes with a pretty big catch for those who have relied on credit card welcome bonuses to earn the Companion Pass. Credit card welcome bonus points will no longer count for the Companion Pass Previously, the Companion Pass was earned with Companion Pass qualifying points, which weren't quite the same as the TQPs used to earn elite status. Most notably, this meant that welcome bonus points earned from signing up for Southwest credit cards counted toward earning the Companion Pass, even though the bonus points didn't count as TQPs toward elite status. This was a really big deal. Welcome bonuses on Southwest credit cards can sometimes get you 80,000 Rapid Rewards points (or even more) once you meet the spending requirements. That has gone a long way toward reaching the 135,000 Companion Pass qualifying points currently needed to earn a Companion Pass. But that strategy is going away starting next year. Southwest's website now states (bolding mine): "Starting January 1, 2027, certain activities that helped you qualify for a Companion Pass by earning Companion Pass qualifying points do not earn Tier Qualifying Points. Therefore, these activities, while still earning Rapid Rewards points, will not assist you in earning Companion Pass benefits. These include new Cardmember welcome bonuses, referral bonuses, anniversary points, and bonus points from spend (e.g., 2x on gas), as well as partner spend (e.g., hotel, car)." In other words, those big credit card welcome bonuses that have helped so many travelers unlock the Companion Pass will no longer get you any closer to earning it beginning in 2027. Travelers who earn a Companion Pass under the existing rules in 2026 will still enjoy its benefits through the end of 2027. Additionally, note that the Southwest FAQs state that: "Cardmembers who are approved for a Rapid Rewards Credit Card on or before Dec. 2, 2026, and meet the requirements for the new Cardmember welcome bonus will have the opportunity to have those points count as Companion Pass qualifying points, even if the spend threshold is met in early 2027." New ways to earn Southwest Companion Pass benefits in 2027 Beginning in 2027, to receive unlimited Companion Pass trips, you'll need to earn 140,000 TQPs or complete 100 qualifying one-way flights to reach Southwest's new Platinum status. There is some good news here, however. Southwest will provide a 10,000-TQP boost once you reach 130,000 earned TQPs in 2027, pushing you to the 140,000 TQPs needed to unlock Platinum status and its Companion Pass benefit for the remainder of 2027 and all of 2028. Southwest is also introducing a new Milestone Reward that provides three Companion Pass trips once you earn 95,000 TQPs or complete 75 qualifying one-way flights. And there's another potentially helpful change for those who can put significant spending on Southwest credit cards. Beginning in 2027, all Southwest credit cards will earn 1 TQP per dollar spent, making it easier to earn elite status — and ultimately Companion Pass benefits — through credit card spending on any of the Southwest credit cards. Of course, that's quite different from earning tens of thousands of qualifying points all at once from a welcome bonus. There's certainly some good news coming out of Southwest Airlines today, but it isn't all good news — especially for travelers who have relied on credit card welcome bonuses to earn the Companion Pass. For years, strategically timing Southwest credit card applications and welcome bonuses has been one of the most popular ways to unlock this valuable perk without spending a fortune on flights. And while Southwest is introducing some new ways to earn companion benefits, including a three-trip Milestone Reward and more TQPs from credit card spending, those changes won't necessarily make up for losing one of the easiest shortcuts to one of the most valuable perks in the world of points and miles. Want to hear more about Southwest's big changes? Watch our Talking Points with TPG discussion that breaks down what travelers need to know.

item.title: The Diplomat Is Back for Season Four—Where Is the Political Thriller Filmed?
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favorite films, television shows, and more. This time, we ask: where was The Diplomat filmed? This story contains major spoilers for season four. Watching The Diplomat is like being a fly on the wall in some of the worldâs most powerful rooms and buildings. But the Netflix series, though often immensely dramatic, rarely puts its characters in places that reflect them intimately. Instead, as production designer Curt Beech explains, The Diplomat is about âbringing the characters together physically but never emotionally in spaces the public donât get to see.â âThe places may be historical, but they're almost never personal,â he says. âThat is what's so different about this show from a design standpoint. Usually, we're creating someone's bedroom or their house, and we dig into their family history and who they are and what they like. We don't get any of that here because the spaces that they inhabit are not theirs. They are almost always visitors.â The fourth season of The Diplomat opens with a bangâliterally. In the first episode, US President Grace Penn, played by Allison Janney, survives an assassination attempt outside Windsor Castle. She becomes increasingly unpredictable afterwards, confusing her husband Todd (Bradley Whitford), Vice President Hal Wyler (Rufus Sewell), and Kate Wyler, the US ambassador to the UK (Keri Russell). The story brings the characters from Windsor Castle to Washington, DC to Lucca, Italy, where it concludes on a cliffhanger at a meeting of the G7. Beech used some of the same locations and sets from past seasons, but also brought new locations to life in England, New York, and Italy. The interior sets were created at Steiner Studios in New York, while Wrotham House returned as Winfield House, the residence of the United States ambassador in London. Here Beech breaks down the key locations from The Diplomat Season 4. Season 4 opens with an impromptu visit to Windsor Castle. As the envoy leaves the British royal residence to fly back to the US, President Penn gets shot by an unknown assailant. Beech combined nine different locations to create Windsor Castle and its grounds. The exterior and inner courtyard were filmed at Burghley House, while Belvoir Castle, Lancaster House and the British Foreign Office were used for interiors. Back in the US, the team filmed at Woolworth Estate, St. Josaphat Monastery Library and Sleepy Hollow Country Club. The grandiose panic room where Kate and Hal are locked down after the shooting was filmed in the crypt of a church on the Upper West Side. âIt's a lot of different architectural styles, but that is typical of these houses,â Beech says. âWindsor has a bunch of things going on because these houses are very, very old, and they've been built during different centuries with different people in charge of the construction. We embraced that. We also have a mix of things that are accurate to Windsor Castle and things that arenât.â After she is shot, President Penn is airlifted in Marine One to a docked United States aircraft carrier for surgery. Beech used the parking lot at Steiner Studios for the helicopter landing, while a Marine training facility in New York City was transformed into the interiors. âWe did real takeoffs and landings with the helicopter,â Beech says. âWhile it was on the ground, we dressed the interior because Marine One feels like a private jet inside. It's very luxurious and well appointed. But you canât add weight to a helicopter like that without going through a lot of different FAA approvals, so we couldnât keep it dressed while flying.â As in the past, Winfield Houseâs exterior was filmed Wrotham Park, an estate in Hertfordshire. Some of the interiors were built at Steiner, while others were filmed inside Wrotham Park. âThere's a blue room, a library, and a red room in the real building,â Beech says. âThe foyer is also there. The green room, the Wedgewood hallway, and the blue study are on stage in New York. It takes a lot of coordination to keep track. The actors are incredible because they're able to tap back into whatever they were doing at that moment two months ago, and make it feel like they just turned the corner and are walking into a room.â The US Embassy in Londonâs Nine Elms was built on a soundstage in London for earlier seasons. The set was shipped to Steiner for Season 3 and rebuilt there. In Season 4, not much has changed. âWe moved some furniture around to get better lighting, but nothing major has changed in those spaces,â Beech says. The production did shoot one scene, a meeting between CIA station chief Eidra Park (Ali Ahn) and deputy chief Stuart Hayford (Ato Essandoh), in Nine Elms. âThat was right around the corner from the embassy, which was incredible to see,â Beech says. âThat building is in so many different shows now and itâs beautiful.â Eidraâs modern apartment, where Stuart eventually moves in as they begin a relationship, was a real apartment in Tribeca. âThis is another space that's personal, but not,â Beech says. âWe told the story that she moves a lot for the safety of her position. Sheâs never in the same place for very long. So itâs very stark and doesnât have a lot of personality.â For Season 4, Beech made some alterations to the White House set. He decided not to use the Oval Office seen in prior seasons and to shift the action into President Pennâs private study. âThe president typically does have a study, and it's right off the Oval Office, but itâs very small,â Beech says. âYou see lots of pictures of Obama sitting in his. We made a very large study for her that has three separate zonesâa work zone, a meeting zone, and a power zone where her desk is. That does not exist in the real White House, but it does in our White House.â In one scene, Todd is swimming laps in the White House pool. That also doesnât exist in real life. The scene was filmed in the basement of the Woolworth Building in Tribeca. âThere used to be a pool years and years ago in the White House,â Beech says. âThey plastered it over, and it's now the press briefing room. But you see in the old pictures there was a really beautiful room with arched windows and thatâs where the pool was.â Although 10 Downing Street has appeared in previous seasons, the set this year was new. âThat was filmed at a location in the UK that was no longer available, so we built it on our stage,â Beech says. âWe also used the Steinway Mansion in New York for the buildingâs iconic stairs.â When a new prime minister comes into power midway through the season, viewers might notice subtle shifts in the dÃ©cor. âIt got a bit more sparse, indicating that she had just gotten there,â Beech says. âThey had moved him out; she hadn't completely moved in yet. So some pictures are off the walls, and the lamp on his desk changed. It's small stuff.â The exterior of 10 Downing Street was filmed outside the British Foreign Office in London. âWe wound up building the doorway and the lectern in a parking lot in Brooklyn with a green screen, and then we added it together with what we shot in London on that street,â Beech explains. Kate goes to meet with the newly-minted British prime minister in the family home of the prime ministerâs husband, offering a rare glimpse into a characterâs private life. Beech used two different locations to create the vast manor house. The entry and gate were shot at Ingatestone Hall in Essex, and the interior was filmed in a house on Long Island. âIn England with these huge estates, it's very expensive to keep them going, so the family compresses to living in one wing of the house,â Beech says. âWe wanted to tell that story about her house, and thereâs a coldness to it. Her office space is in a room that is gigantic for an office. And there are heaters everywhere.â The season concludes with a tumultuous visit to Lucca, Italy, where the members of the G7 are holding a summit. The production went to Lucca for six weeks to film in eight different locations. These included Villa Viesca, the former summer home of Salvatore and Wanda Ferragamo, and Dimora Ghirlandaio, a resort in Tuscany, both of which comprised the villas where the American envoy stays during the summit. The G7 meetings were held at the recently restored Villa Reale di Marlia, Villa Medici in Poggio a Caiano, and Villa Medicea La Petraia. âWe were going play Florence for Lucca, but we leaned into Lucca as Lucca, and it felt better and more authentic,â Beech says. âWe went to the Pitti Palace in Florence and determined that it wasn't right. Most of the time, the vibe is very modern in these meetings. We decided to make it very classical. We embraced the vibe of this incredible room with floor-to-ceiling frescoes, and we built custom desks that had little fresco elements that matched the walls. These meetings are very bespoke, so everything is always created for them. We did that, but in a slightly different manner.â

item.title: How to redeem Choice Privileges points
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Earning Choice Privileges points through stays, promotions and credit cards is relatively easy. However, once you have a stash of Choice Privileges points, you might wonder how to redeem them. As with most points and miles, the value you'll get when redeeming Choice points will vary. TPG's October 2026 valuations peg the value of Choice points at 0.85 cents each, so we typically recommend aiming for at least that redemption value. Choice offers different redemption options depending on your country of residence, but here's what U.S. residents need to know about redeeming Choice Privileges points. You'll typically get the most value from Choice Privileges points when you redeem them for hotel stays. There are three primary ways to do this: reward nights, points-plus-cash stays and Preferred Hotels & Resorts stays. Reward nights start at 6,000 points, though most properties require at least 8,000 points per night. You may also find discounted reward nights through Choice's RewardSaver program. If you want to stay at a particular property, you can check award availability and pricing by clicking on the check-in date box. When redeeming Choice points, you can often book more than just the base room type at many properties. For example, at the Quality Inn Bastrop in Texas, you can often book a room that can sleep up to six guests for the same number of points as a room that can sleep up to two. You can book far more than Choice-branded hotels with Choice points, though. For example, you can use Choice Privileges points to stay at select Bluegreen Vacations properties. Note that there's usually a two-night minimum stay. You can also book Westgate Resorts properties with Choice points. Most properties have a two-night minimum stay, but they are another option if you're looking for more space than most hotel rooms provide. Additionally, you can redeem Choice points for stays at participating Radisson-family hotels in the Americas but not the rest of the world. You can use Choice points to book select casino hotels and resorts as well. Check here for the current casino properties you can book with Choice points. You can also book all-inclusive resorts with Choice Privileges points. At the time of writing, Choice points are redeemable at all-inclusive resorts in Mexico and the Dominican Republic. Choice Titanium members receive a Titanium travel award that provides a 50% discount on one qualifying reward night reservation each year. This travel award is valid for a stay of up to seven nights in a single room at participating properties and must be used within the same calendar year it was awarded. Choice also offers points plus cash rates if you have at least 6,000 Choice points in your account. Log in to your account, search for a reward night and select a result that shows a points-plus-cash rate. Once you click "See Availability" for the property you want to book, you can compare the reward night, the points-plus-cash rate and paid rates for each room type. In the above example, you could pay 15,000 points, $142 or 6,000 points plus $77 per night for a rate that allows you to cancel until shortly before your stay. If you redeem 15,000 points, you will get a redemption rate of 0.95 cents per point. If you redeem 6,000 points plus $77, you'd use fewer points and get a better redemption rate of 1.08 cents per point. You're effectively buying points with the cash portion of a points-plus-cash rate. So, you won't earn any points on points-plus-cash stays. And if you cancel, you'll be refunded the full number of points used for the reservation, including those you bought with the cash portion of the booking. You can only buy up to 250,000 points per calendar year by booking points-plus-cash rates. Choice Privileges members can redeem Choice points for stays at participating Preferred Hotels & Resorts properties. For single or double occupancy, you can expect to redeem 20,000 to 250,000 points per night. You can browse properties and book stays online by starting at this link and logging into your Choice Privileges account. Transfer Choice points to travel rewards partners You can use the online Choice Privileges Rewards Exchange to transfer points to the following partners: - Aeromexico Rewards: Convert at a ratio of 5,000 Choice points to 1,000 Aeromexico points - Air Canada Aeroplan: Convert at a ratio of 5,000 Choice points to 1,000 Aeroplan points - Air France-KLM Flying Blue: Convert at a ratio of 5,000 Choice points to 1,000 Flying Blue miles - Alaska Airlines Atmos Rewards: Convert at a ratio of 5,000 Choice points to 1,000 Atmos Rewards points - Avianca Lifemiles: Convert at a ratio of 5,000 Choice points to 1,000 Avianca miles - LATAM Pass: Convert at a ratio of 5,000 Choice points to 1,000 LATAM miles - Qantas Frequent Flyer: Convert at a ratio of 2,000 Choice points to 800 Qantas points - Saudia AlFursan: Convert at a ratio of 5,000 Choice points to 1,000 Saudia miles - Southwest Rapid Rewards: Convert at a ratio of 6,000 Choice points to 1,800 Southwest points - Turkish Miles&Smiles: Convert at a ratio of 5,000 Choice points to 1,000 Turkish miles - United MileagePlus: Convert at a ratio of 5,000 Choice points to 1,000 United miles - Velocity Frequent Flyer: Convert at a ratio of 2,000 Choice points to 800 Virgin Australia points Transfers usually occur within 72 hours but may take up to seven days. You can also redeem Choice points for many types of gift cards. You can usually redeem 8,000 Choice points for a $25 gift card, 16,000 points for a $50 gift card and 32,000 points for a $100 gift card. However, you'll usually only get 0.31 cents per point when redeeming Choice points for gift cards. This is below the value you can typically get when redeeming points for stays, so we typically don't recommend redeeming Choice points for gift cards. Redeem Choice points for an AARP membership You can also redeem Choice points for a one- or three-year AARP membership. A one-year membership costs 5,000 points, while a three-year membership costs 12,000 points. A one-year membership typically costs $20, while a three-year membership costs $55. So, you'd be getting 0.4 to 0.46 cents per point. Transfer Choice points to another member You can transfer Choice points to another member via the Choice website if both accounts have been open for at least 30 days and you have at least 5,000 points in your account. There's no cost to transfer points to another member. You must transfer at least 5,000 points per transfer, but you can only transfer in increments of 1,000 points, and there's a maximum of 100,000 points per transfer. You can also only transfer up to 200,000 points per calendar year and receive up to 100,000 points per calendar year. Exchange Choice points for cruise credits It's possible to redeem Choice points for cruise credit when you book by phone with Cruises for Choice Privileges (powered by Cruise411) at 800-596-0451. You can redeem 85,000 points for $250 in cruise credit or 160,000 points for $500 in cruise credit. However, you'll only get a redemption rate of 0.29 to 0.31 cents per point when redeeming for cruise credits. You can also redeem Choice points for college sports experiences, NASCAR tickets, concerts and other events on the Experiences by Choice website. Most of the options are experiences you can bid on rather than buy outright. Finally, you can donate Choice points to select charities. Choice will donate $5 per 1,000 points redeemed to most charities. However, if you donate your points to Polaris, Choice will donate $10 per 1,000 points. You'll typically get the most value from your Choice Privileges points when redeeming them for hotel stays. However, with options ranging from budget-friendly hotels to upscale resorts, it's worth comparing award rates with paid rates before redeeming. Although you can also use Choice points for airline miles, gift cards, cruises and other rewards, most of these options provide less value than TPG's October 2026 valuation of 0.85 cents per point. I'd generally recommend saving your Choice points for hotel stays where you can get at least that much value. Terms & restrictions apply. See rates & fees.

item.title: How a Missed Turnaround on Mt. Shasta Turned a Dayhike into a 36-Hour Survival Situation
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine
How Backpacker reported this story: Writer Sam Anderson spoke with the Forest Service program manager for Shasta’s climbing rangers and the Siskiyou County Sheriff’s Office to learn about how two dayhikers ended up spending 36 hours stuck high on California’s Mt. Shasta and the mission to rescue them. Two hikers from Salt Lake City had a close call on Mt. Shasta this week after a missed turnaround and a wrong turn forced them to spend an unplanned night exposed to 15-degree weather. The Siskiyou County Sheriff’s Office (SCSO) received a distress call at 10:20 p.m. on Monday, October 12. A 19-year-old male and 20-year-old female were underequipped to safely wait out the night at their location, about 11,000 feet up Avalanche Gulch. They’d begun their day at 4 a.m. at the Bunny Flat Trailhead with no plans to summit, alongside a male companion who did plan to summit. According to Sage Milestone, public information officer for the SCSO, the group had been on their way to Mt. Rainier when they made the spur-of-the-moment decision to climb Shasta. Their route was dangerous from the beginning: Avalanche Gulch’s terraced scree ramps are loose and crumbly without snow and ice to consolidate them. Along with that advisory, the pair had also ignored a recommended turnaround time posted at the trailhead. On their way up, Milestone said, the pair ran into their friend who had summited as he descended; he advised them to turn around at Red Banks, located at 12,800 ft. Unfortunately, the pair did not reach that point until around 5 p.m., five hours past the posted turnaround of noon. Now separated from their companion and stuck in rapidly-dropping temperatures with inadequate clothing, they followed officials’ advice to keep descending to maintain body heat. The group again contacted emergency services at 2 a.m. to report that they had reached Helen Lake at approximately 10,400 feet. Shortly thereafter, their phones died. Rescuers scrambled in a first-light operation involving air and ground operations. Ground searchers and air crews with CHP Air Operations first scanned the upper reaches of Avalanche Canyon. Around 9 a.m., they located two hikers, who turned out to be unrelated to the search and in no need of help. On the ground, crews tried another approach. Beginning at Horse Camp, a large cabin at 7,880 ft. on one of the mountain’s most prominent trails, which the hikers had already passed on their way up, they descended into nearby Cascade Gulch. While rescuers didn’t necessarily think Cascade Gulch was the most likely place to find the missing climbers, searching it was a matter of diligence, Nick Meyers, program manager for the Forest Service’s Mt. Shasta climbing rangers and avalanche center, said. “Cascade Gulch is a common place for people to end up if they get lost on Avalanche, but it’s usually only when the trails are covered,” Meyers said. “When trails are exposed like they are now, you can just follow the main drainage to hit any of the trails back to Bunny Flat.” However low-percentage, the decision paid off. Rescuers in Cascade Gulch heard shouting around 4 p.m. Soon they had located the two hikers, who were uninjured and managed to descend safely with help. According to rescue crews, the hikers confirmed they had passed Horse Camp on their way down. How they got lost from there remained unclear. “The trail from the cabin to Bunny Flats is a superhighway,” Meyers explained. “It’s the baseline recommended day hike for anyone of any experience level on that area of the mountain, so it’s really well-marked and very wide. We’re still scratching our heads about how they missed it.” While Milestone said “there were red flags from the get-go on [the hikers’] attempt,” he noted that officials were grateful the climbers followed rangers’ advice to keep moving down the mountain to stay warm, and that they believed the pair had learned from their experience. The rescue follows multiple similar incidents on Mt. Shasta during the past month. One badly injured hiker was airlifted from Horse Camp on Sept. 11 after attempting a glissade at high altitude, injuring his feet, and crawling back down most of Avalanche Gulch. And three young hikers endured a long rescue in early September after using AI to plan their summit bid via the Clear Creek route.

item.title: Fast-growing Viking adds 7 more new ships from Europe to Egypt
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Fast-growing Viking adds 7 more new ships from Europe to Egypt One of the greatest growth stories in the history of cruising continued on Thursday as Viking unveiled yet another large crop of new vessels. The 29-year-old cruise brand officially welcomed seven new ships to its fleet during an intimate naming ceremony along the waterfront of Amsterdam, bringing its total to 109. The addition of the new vessels, all designed for river cruising, puts Viking firmly in the top spot among cruise companies of the world for the title of the cruise company with the most ships. The nearest competitor in terms of total ship count is Carnival Corporation, which currently operates 92 vessels among its eight brands after reducing its fleet size in recent years from a high of 104 ships. Carnival Corporation is the parent company of Carnival Cruise Line, Princess Cruises and Holland America, among other major lines. "We are very proud to celebrate our seven newest river ships, and as we approach Viking's 30th anniversary in 2027, our best years are still ahead of us," Viking CEO and president Leah Talactac said at the event, which began with pierside festivities and ended with a gala dinner at Amsterdam's historic Koepelkerk. More than 100 Viking executives, port officials, business partners and media were on hand for the event, which included a performance by Sissel Kyrkjebø, one of the world's leading crossover sopranos, and Norwegian violinist Tor Jaran Apold. Only two of the seven new vessels, the 190-passenger Viking Rota and 190-passenger Viking Haki, were physically present in Amsterdam for the naming ceremony. Both ships will sail on Europe's Rhine, Main and Danube rivers, with itineraries that often begin or end in Amsterdam. Three of the seven new ships were located on the two rivers where they will be sailing, the Nile in Egypt and the Seine in France. Two more were at the Neptun Werft shipyard in Rostock, Germany, where they were undergoing the last stages of construction. Still, the captains and godmothers (and, in a couple of cases, godfathers) of all seven vessels were present at the pierside event for the ceremony, which included video feeds from each of the vessels as, one by one, they were officially named with a smash of Norwegian aquavit against their hulls. The use of bottles of aquavit instead of bottles of Champagne to name the vessels was a nod to Viking's Norwegian heritage. (Viking founder Torstein Hagen is Norwegian.) All seven of the godmothers and godfathers for the ships were owners or top executives of travel advisor companies that sell Viking cruises. Thursday's event was just the latest milestone in what has been an extraordinary period of growth for Viking. With the addition of the seven new river ships, Viking now operates 94 river ships around the world, as well as 13 traditional ocean ships and two expedition cruise vessels. As recently as 2012, the company fielded just 29 river ships and not a single ocean ship. The recently public company, which now has more than 12,000 employees, has been one of the fastest-growing cruise companies in history and shows no signs of slowing its growth. As Viking executives noted in a briefing for media on Thursday before the naming event, the company has 36 more river ships on order or under option for delivery by 2032 — an astounding number. It also has 17 ocean ships on order or under option for delivery by 2034. The latter total includes two additional expedition cruise ships the company has ordered for delivery in 2030 and 2031. The additions will further cement Viking's position as the fastest growing major cruise company in terms of number of ships. Still, while Viking is adding ships faster than its biggest cruise company competitors, it still carries significantly fewer passengers per year than several of them, including industry giants Carnival Corporation and Royal Caribbean Group, as its average ship size is considerably smaller. That said, by one other significant measure, Viking is now bigger than Carnival Corporation, which long dominated the cruise world by almost every metric from ship count and passenger capacity to profitability. As of Thursday's close, Viking's stock market capitalization, at $37.4 billion, had pulled ahead of Carnival Corporation's market capitalization by nearly a billion dollars. Royal Caribbean Group, the parent company of Royal Caribbean, Celebrity Cruises and Silversea Cruises, currently has the biggest stock market capitalization among cruise companies with a value as of Thursday's close of nearly $75 billion. Viking has seen enormous success since its founding 29 years ago with intimate, upscale cruises aimed at the 55-plus traveler — a segment of travelers that has more time and money for travel than younger segments of the traveling population. Designed for the "thinking person," as founder Hagen likes to say, they are trips that revolve heavily around the destinations that the ships visit, with longer stays in ports that allow for more in-depth exploring and included tours in every port. In the case of the line's ocean ships, they also feature expert lecturers on board to explain the things passengers are seeing. All Viking cruises, notably, are adults-only, with no children under the age of 18 allowed — something that is rare in the world of cruising. On many sailings, most passengers are retirees. Viking ships also are particularly known for their elegant, Scandinavian-influenced design, which is modern, upscale and residential in its feel. It is a combination that has proved to be hugely popular. Thanks to strong demand for its cruises and its rapid expansion in ships to meet the demand, Viking is now the leader by far in river cruises for North Americans with 52% of the market. It accounts for about 27% of the market for luxury ocean cruises, which also makes it the leader in that space. The seven new river ships that Viking welcomed on Thursday include four — Viking Rota, Viking Haki, Viking Halogi and Viking Sjofn — that will sail the brand's most popular itineraries along Europe's Rhine, Main and Danube rivers. item.title: Where Was ‘Tenzing’ Filmed? Inside the Extreme Alpine Locations Across Nepal and New Zealand.
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine
In 1953, Tenzing Norgay, alongside mountaineer Edmund Hillary, made the first ascent of Mount Everest. Usually, the names are reversed, but Tenzing—Apple TV’s new feature film about the first summit of the world’s highest mountain—takes this historic mountaineering figure out of the shadow and into the foreground. Both men stood on the 29,032-foot peak together, but Tenzing, a highly experienced Nepali-Indian Sherpa who spent two decades pioneering Himalayan routes, had not been the main focus of this moment in mountaineering history until now. The first ascent of Everest has often been told as a story of British achievement, as it was funded by the Royal Geographical Society, without much focus on the Himalayan climber’s role and his little-known origin story. The film’s director Jennifer Peedom first traveled to Everest more than 20 years ago and said in her director’s statement she left changed by the people who work in its shadow. Her 2015 documentary Sherpa focuses on the lives of Himalayan guides and the human side of mountaineering around Mount Everest. Now Tenzing, her first feature film, shifts the focus to Tenzing Norgay (Genden Phuntsok), who made history alongside Edmund Hillary (Tom Hiddleston) in an authentic, visceral film that rejected green screens and studio sets. Instead, the crew shot in sub-zero alpine conditions across Nepal and New Zealand, capturing treacherous climbing footage on real glaciers, rock walls, and crevasses. The production across these two countries ultimately connects Tenzing’s heritage in Nepal with Hillary’s national significance in New Zealand where he was from. We sat down with Tenzing’s cinematographer, Stefan Duscio, to find out what it was like to recreate the historic first summit of Mount Everest, filming in extreme environments. In 2024, Peedom and Duscio scouted locations across Nepal to establish Tenzing’s early life on the Tibetan Plateau, Nepal, and India. They intended to capture cultural and lower-elevation scenes in Nepal, while taking the technical alpine sequences to the Southern Alps of New Zealand. “We wanted to use Nepal to represent all three of those countries. We wanted to do as much of the movie as possible in Nepal, and then really only take the high-altitude alpine sequences to New Zealand because it was safer to film those there at a lower altitude,” Duscio tells Outside. The New Zealand peaks are at a low-enough elevation that oxygen wasn’t needed while filming on them. The filmmakers enlisted veteran New Zealand mountaineer Guy Cotter, CEO of Adventure Consultants and an Everest expedition leader of 25 years, as mountain safety supervisor. He was part of the first commercially guided expedition on Everest in 1992. Cotter suggested the region around Aoraki, also known as Mount Cook, in the South Island of New Zealand, to be a good match for the Himalayas and Everest. “Guy is intimately familiar with both landscapes,” says Duscio. “So Jen and I worked with him to help understand those alpine locations and to get his advice on: What do you think is a really good match for the Western Cwm or what’s a really good match for Base Camp or Advanced Base Camp, or the Lhotse Face?” Duscio says they found close approximations in the Aoraki region to double for all their Everest locations. New Zealand’s Aoraki still has extensive glaciers, icefalls, and seracs. They found an approximation of the Khumbu Icefall in New Zealand: the Darwin Icefall. New Zealand’s stand-in locations for Everest certainly didn’t make the filming easy by any means. It dropped to negative negative 13 degrees Fahrenheit (negative 25 degrees Celsius) during filming in some locations in New Zealand. Duscio says he remembers some of the mountaineers, like Cotter in particular, say they were wearing more layers here than they would on an Everest expedition. “It was tough… but we were safe,” says Duscio. “The struggle was real, though.” Western climbers often see Everest as something to be conquered, but Tenzing revered the mountain, which the Tibetans and Sherpas call Chomolungma, as the sacred mother goddess. It was a lifelong dream and a spiritual calling for Tenzing to climb Everest. And high above the world, with its class structures and social divisions, he found mutual respect and trust with Hillary Tenzing’s early life was filmed in Nepal’s Lower Mustang region, a high-altitude desert near Nepal’s northern border. “That was a great double for the Tibetan Plateau because the geology there just feels ancient,” says Duscio. “The rock faces, the mountains are absolutely enormous, and it felt like a really good approximation of what his childhood would have looked like there. The ancient village of Dangarjong felt like it had been untouched for hundreds of years.” Filming in Nepal also meant carrying the responsibility of portraying a revered national figure. “Tenzing’s a national hero over there, and he looms large,” says Duscio. “A lot of people love him and respect him, and so when they’d hear about our film, they had a lot of questions.” The most common one was, “Who’s playing Tenzing?” “They wanted to make sure he spoke their language and wasn’t some Hollywood star,” says Duscio. Genden Phuntsok had never climbed a mountain when Jennifer Peedom cast him in Apple’s ‘Tenzing.’ He talks to us about what it took to carry a film about the first ascent of Everest. Read the interview here. Duscio, five film crew members, and porters had special permission from the Nepali government to film at Everest Base Camp outside of the climbing season. After hiking through the Khumbu Valley, the team camped at Base Camp to shoot landscapes from the ground, drones, and helicopters. “We wanted anyone who’s climbed Everest to feel like it was very accurate,” says Duscio. The production also cast 12 Sherpa climbers who took the climbing season off to work on the film, which added another level to the authenticity of what a real Everest expedition is like. “Between them, our 12 Sherpa cast members had summited Everest over 65 times,” Duscio says. Beyond being cast members, they offered their expertise to make sure the production was safe. One of the film’s most physically demanding sequences recreates the moment Hillary slips into a crevasse, leaving Tenzing to self-arrest with his ice axe and haul him to safety. “It was very taxing to film, and it took months to plan it as everyone was nervous about putting actors and crew in a real crevasse and a real icefall, says Duscio. Both Phuntsok and Hiddleston filmed the sequence anchored by safety lines. “Tom was very keen to prove he could cut steps and climb out. He sort of needed to swing his body to get momentum to start cutting steps,” Duscio says. The sequence toward the end of the film where Tenzing and Hillary have to climb the ice face to get to the summit was also one of the cinematographer’s most intense scenes to capture. They filmed it in the highest ridgelines on the Remarkables mountain range near Queenstown, New Zealand, to recreate the Hillary Step—the iconic 40-foot vertical rock face on Everest’s southeast ridge. “It was vertigo-inducing,” Duscio recalls. “It was so high and hectic, and I could barely stand with a camera next to the cast. It was really impressive what [the actors] achieved there, but we wanted it to be very dramatic and showcase their athleticism,” notes Duscio. Filming in the homelands of Tenzing and Hillary across Nepal and New Zealand mirrored the historic bond between the two climbers. Hillary is a national hero in New Zealand, just as Tenzing is in Nepal. “Shooting in both homelands was a wonderful parallel,”says Duscio. The two climbers became lifelong friends, and the Aoraki region contains the mountains that Hillary trained on as a young man. The connection came full circle when Tenzing’s son, Norbu Tenzing, visited the alpine set in New Zealand and was formally welcomed by local Māori leaders, bridging the shared legacy of the two climbers who reached the top of the world together. “There were just so many beautiful moments of synchronicity where you could feel the heritage of Tenzing and Hillary blessing our film,” says Duscio.

item.title: The definitive guide to American Express Global Dining Access by Resy
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
The definitive guide to American Express Global Dining Access by Resy If you're an eligible Amex cardmember, you have access to American Express Global Dining Access by Resy. This collection can net you savings at some of the world's best restaurants and may even qualify you for your card's U.S. Resy statement credit if it has one. This isn't a perk that's often discussed, so it's easy to forget about. Here's what you need to know. What is Global Dining Access by Resy? Global Dining Access by Resy is a portfolio of restaurants worldwide that partner with Amex to offer top-tier cardmembers premium dining experiences at some of the best spots in town. You can get prime restaurant reservations, even at venues that show as fully booked. Many of the restaurants have earned Michelin stars or are consistently ranked among the best in their respective cities. While reservations aren't always guaranteed, it's always good to know you have this benefit in your back pocket. It could make the difference between snagging a seat at a bucket-list restaurant or missing out. Which cards are eligible for Global Dining Access by Resy? Since this is an exclusive perk for certain cardmembers, you'll need to have one of the following cards: - Business Centurion Card from American Express* - Corporate Platinum Card® from American Express* - Corporate Centurion Card® from American Express* - The Platinum Card® from American Express Exclusively for Morgan Stanley* - The Platinum Card® from American Express Exclusively for Charles Schwab* - The Platinum Card® from American Express for Goldman Sachs* - The Centurion® Card from American Express for Goldman Sachs* Even if you don't currently have one of those cards, you can still browse the list of restaurants and take note of places you may want to visit in the future. *The information for these cards has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer. How does Global Dining Access by Resy work? The easiest places for cardmembers to access Global Dining Access by Resy and make a reservation are through the Resy app and on resy.com. Once an eligible Amex card is linked to your Resy account, you'll see your Global Dining Access benefits in Resy. (Cardmembers can also call the Amex concierge to get this set up.) Keep in mind that you'll be subject to each restaurant's cancellation policy, which varies by establishment. Global Dining Access includes restaurants in the U.S., Italy and Peru. Only one city per country is currently featured for Italy and Peru. Not all American cities are covered by the program, but most major cities should have some participating restaurants. As we mentioned earlier, this collection includes some of the world's top restaurants, so you'll definitely want to check out the full list on Resy's site. Select American Express cards that have access to Global Dining Access by Resy also come with a statement credit for U.S. Resy purchases. These include: - The American Express Platinum: Earn up to $400 each calendar year in statement credits for purchases made at U.S. Resy restaurants (up to $100 quarterly; enrollment required). - The Delta SkyMiles Reserve American Express Card and the Delta SkyMiles Reserve Business American Express Card: Earn up to $240 each calendar year in statement credits for purchases made at U.S. Resy restaurants (up to $20 monthly; enrollment required). By combining these two benefits, you can get a lot of value out of your next visit to a prestigious restaurant. Whatever restaurant you choose, remember to use a card that earns you bonus points on dining. Even though you'll need to have one of the aforementioned cards to have Global Dining Access, you're not required to pay for your meal with that card. In fact, you probably shouldn't, as there are other cards available that earn more on dining purchases. The only exception is if you're using your eligible Amex card's U.S. Resy statement credit, since you'll need to pay with that card to take advantage of the credit.

item.title: How to transfer Hyatt points online to another member
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
How to transfer Hyatt points online to another member Many loyalty programs don't let you transfer points to other members, while others charge a fee to move points to another member. But with World of Hyatt, members can gift points to other members for free and with few restrictions. That's right: Hyatt members can transfer points to other members without paying a fee. And the program just made it easier to do so. Here's what you need to know about transferring Hyatt points to other members. Can you transfer Hyatt points to another person? You can transfer Hyatt points in your account to any other World of Hyatt member as long as you and the other member have active accounts that have been open for at least 60 days. No family or household affiliation is required, but you can gift Hyatt points from your account to another only once per calendar month and up to six times per calendar year. Similarly, you can receive Hyatt points from another account only once per calendar month and up to six times per calendar year. There's no cost to transfer Hyatt points to another member. However, you can only transfer up to 525,000 points per calendar year and receive up to 525,000 points per calendar year. You must transfer at least 1,000 points per transfer, but transfers are otherwise available in 500-point increments. How to gift Hyatt points to another member Before this, if you wanted to transfer Hyatt points from your account to someone else's, you had to undertake a convoluted process that involved downloading a PDF and emailing it back to Hyatt. Now you can transfer Hyatt points to another member much faster via an online process. Head to Hyatt's purchase, share and gift page, and click on the "Gift your points" link. Doing so will take you to the Hyatt gifting page on points.com's website. Here, you can select how many Hyatt points to gift. On the next page, you'll need to enter the World of Hyatt number, first name, last name and email address of the person to whom you want to gift Hyatt points. For a successful transfer, the details you enter should match the information on their Hyatt account. You can enter an email address on the next page for your confirmation email, and check the box to accept the terms. Double-check the recipient's account information and the number of points you're transferring before submitting your request, as Hyatt's terms state that transfers are final. Once you submit the transfer request, you'll see a confirmation page and get a confirmation email. Hyatt says points generally transfer within 24 hours, but may take up to 10 business days if additional review is needed. However, when I tested out the new digital transfer process, the points were posted to the recipient's account immediately. When should you gift Hyatt points to another person? Gifting points might seem like an excellent idea if you're planning a vacation with other World of Hyatt members. While there are some great Hyatt Category 1 hotels, higher-category properties can require significantly more points under the current Hyatt award chart. Transferring points into a single account from which you can redeem them can bring these more expensive award stays within reach. Pooling your points with friends or family could also allow you to redeem Hyatt points for an upgraded room or to book a longer stay than might otherwise be possible. You might also consider transferring your Hyatt points to another member to prevent them from expiring. You'll forfeit your World of Hyatt points if your account is inactive for 24 consecutive months, but transferring points counts as account activity. You can also currently transfer Bilt Points to Hyatt at a 1:1 ratio. However, this ratio will drop to 4:3 on Jan. 1, 2027. If you want to earn Hyatt points directly, consider the World of Hyatt Credit Card (see rates and fees) or the World of Hyatt Business Credit Card (see rates and fees). Both cards offer valuable welcome offers and let you earn Hyatt points when making purchases. World of Hyatt has long allowed members to transfer points to each other for free, but the new digital process makes this benefit much easier to use. Whether you're pooling points with friends or family for a more expensive award stay or simply topping off another member's account, being able to complete the transfer via an easy online process is a welcome improvement. item.title: Traveling to Europe? Don’t fall for this visa scam
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Since Europe launched its automated border control system, you may have heard about another new addition for travelers: The European Travel Information and Authorisation System, or ETIAS, which will require many tourists to obtain a waiver before entering most continental European countries. You may even have seen websites offering these waivers. Don’t take the bait. Since Europe is still grappling with the disastrous rollout of EES, the ETIAS has been postponed until at least 2027. These waivers are not required or available yet, but scammers don’t want you to know that. Read on to learn more about ETIAS, what you actually need to enter Europe right now and how to stay safe online. What is ETIAS? ETIAS is a forthcoming system that will be used to allow visitors to enter 30 countries in Europe’s Schengen Zone. These include popular tourist destinations like France, Germany, Greece, Switzerland and Spain; see the full list here. When the system goes live, travelers from dozens of visa-exempt countries, including the U.S., will need to apply for an ETIAS travel authorization. It's technically not a visa, but an electronic waiver will allow you to stay in the 30 applicable countries for up to 90 days within any 180-day period. It will be valid for three years or until the travel document you used in your application expires, whichever comes first. The planned cost of an ETIAS waiver is 20 euros (around $22) per adult; travelers under 18 and over 70 can apply for free. How is ETIAS different from the U.K. ETA? ETIAS is easily confused with the United Kingdom’s electronic travel authorisation (ETA), but there is a big difference. When introduced, ETIAS will apply to 30 Schengen Zone countries across continental Europe (and Iceland). It does not apply to the U.K. or Ireland. An ETA, on the other hand, is an existing document that most tourists need to enter the U.K., Jersey, Guernsey or the Isle of Man. It costs 20 pounds ($26) and allows access to these areas for up to six months. While ETIAS is not yet available, you can (and should) apply for an ETA if you are visiting the U.K. The short answer? You can’t — yet. ETIAS was slated to roll out soon after Europe introduced its biometric border control Entry/Exit System. However, EES has been plagued by software bugs and long delays since its launch earlier this year, and as a result, ETIAS has been put on hold until sometime in 2027. Per an official EU site, “ETIAS is currently not in operation and no applications for travel authorisations are collected at this point.” That means travelers to Europe don’t need to do anything at the moment. Keep an eye on the site, and when ETIAS is rolled out, you will need to apply before visiting one of the applicable countries. But until then, nothing is changing about the entry process. Unfortunately, scammers are trying to take advantage of the ETIAS delay by setting up fake websites that prey on travelers. So, the main thing you need to know right now is how to avoid scams. Although ETIAS has not been introduced yet, that hasn’t stopped various websites — over 150 of them — from trying to sell “ETIAS waivers.” These sites often try to hoodwink travelers by mimicking the layout and domain name of the official EU website and creating a false sense of urgency. They may also provide inaccurate information about ETIAS and who needs to apply for it. For now, if you stumble across a site offering ETIAS waivers, it is a scam. ETIAS is not operational yet, and you do not need to apply for a European travel waiver until at least next year. If you do, you will likely end up giving money or personal information to bad actors. The main takeaway is: Do not apply for an ETIAS waiver right now. Instead, keep an eye on this page to see when ETIAS launches, at which point you will most likely need to apply for an ETIAS authorization before you visit the Schengen Zone. When you do, be sure to apply through the official EU website only. According to pan-European border agency Frontex, commercial sites can legitimately apply for ETIAS waivers on behalf of clients, but they may charge exorbitant fees, do dubious things with your data and even put you at risk of identity theft. Stay safe out there.

item.title: How to protect yourself during Florida's ongoing dengue fever outbreak
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
How to protect yourself during Florida's ongoing dengue fever outbreak The Sunshine State is in the middle of a dengue fever outbreak. Florida health officials recently reported more than 250 locally acquired dengue fever cases in 2026 so far, most of them in Hillsborough County, home to Tampa. According to the Journal of Emergency Medical Services, the outbreak "appears to be the largest in several decades in the continental United States." The outbreak has prompted a state of local emergency in Hillsborough County and its neighbors, with workers applying insecticide "day and night" to combat the mosquitoes that transmit the disease. If you're heading to Florida soon or planning a trip, here's what you should consider. What is dengue fever? Dengue, pronounce DEHN-gay and nicknamed "breakbone fever" for the excruciating pain it can cause, is a viral infection spread by mosquitoes in tropical and subtropical climates. Most infected individuals experience mild or no symptoms and will recover on their own in a week or two, though they may feel fatigued for several weeks afterward. However, some patients develop severe dengue, which can be life-threatening and requires hospitalization. Individuals who have had dengue in the past are at a higher risk of contracting severe dengue. There is currently no cure for dengue; patients are treated with pain management. Dengue has spread rapidly in recent decades, in part due to climate change: Rising temperatures extend the mosquito breeding season and accelerate the growth of mosquito larvae. As a result, dengue is spreading to new areas that used to be too chilly for mosquitoes, including parts of Europe and the Eastern Mediterranean. According to WHO, 2024 saw a record-breaking dengue year, with over 14.6 million reported cases and 12,000-plus deaths around the globe. Some parts of Florida have historically been a dengue risk, but the current outbreak increased your chances of catching the virus, especially if you are heading to the Tampa area. This doesn't mean you should cancel your plans, but you should be extra cautious. There is no widely available vaccine for dengue. Because the virus is primarily spread by mosquitoes, your best bet is to avoid bites by wearing protective clothing and bug spray while outdoors. I personally recommend permethrin, which you can apply to your clothes before you travel. Once dried, this waterproof bug repellant has no odor or oily feel, and it will stay on through several washes. In mosquito-prone areas, I wear permethrin-treated pants and long sleeves, then apply bug spray to any exposed areas. While visiting Florida, keep an eye out for dengue symptoms, including: - severe headache or pain behind the eyes If you exhibit these symptoms, there's a good chance they can be self-managed and will go away in one to two weeks. However, if you develop symptoms of severe dengue — which often present after the fever subsides — you should seek medical attention immediately: Dengue is not spread person-to-person, so you don't have to worry about giving the virus to your travel companions. Florida draws countless tourists to its beaches, theme parks and natural wonders like the Everglades. But it's also home to pesky, disease-carrying mosquitoes — which are active year-round due to the state's warm climate. The current dengue outbreak should not stop you from traveling this winter, but you should take appropriate precautions. Pack the right clothes and bug repellant to protect yourself from mosquitoes, and know the symptoms of dengue in the unlikely event that you need medical attention. That way, you can travel safely and stress-free.

item.title: 6 amazing excursions you’ll only find on an Alaska cruisetour
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
6 amazing excursions you’ll only find on an Alaska cruisetour Alaska is a gigantic playground for outdoor enthusiasts, offering once-in-a-lifetime adventures unique to the 49th state. During an Alaska cruise, you can book a helicopter ride to land on a glacier and go dogsledding or take a journey on the historic narrow gauge railroad, the White Pass & Yukon Route Railway (also known as "The Scenic Railway of the World"), in Skagway; take a floatplane into a remote location for a bear-viewing adventure from Anchorage; or go crabbing in Ketchikan on the famed Aleutian Ballad from the Discovery Channel show "Deadliest Catch." If that's not enough excitement, you can ramp up the thrill level a few more notches with these six adventure-filled excursions. They are only available if you've booked a cruisetour (a type of package that combines a cruise with a multinight land-based tour) to Alaska and will be heading north to Denali and Fairbanks — or are independently traveling to the National Park and Fairbanks before or after your cruise. Large cruise lines offering cruisetours include Princess Cruises, Holland America Line, Celebrity Cruises and Norwegian Cruise Lines. Since these are small group tours and specialty excursions with limited space, you'll want to reserve them as far in advance as possible. Also make note of the cancellation policy when booking in case you need to alter your travel plans. It's important to know that several cruise lines can offer the same or similar excursions, however, the physical and age requirements may be different — and the pricing can vary. If you're comfortable going it on your own, consider contacting the tour provider or outfitter directly to book the excursion as the pricing may be lower. Search for bears and other wildlife in Denali National Park & Preserve The National Park Service offers several excursions that you can book through its website, and the tours range from five to 13 hours. with costs starting at around $144 per person ($65.00 for kids 15 and younger). The approximately 5 1/2-hour narrated "Tundra Wilderness Tour" is the most popular outing. It offers some of the best wildlife viewing opportunities to see Denali's "Big Five:" brown (or grizzly) bears, moose, wolves, Dall sheep and caribou. If you want to spend a full day in Denali, learn about the park's history from a NPS Interpretive Ranger and visit the old mining town of Kantishna (which gives you multiple chances to see the "Big Five"), book the "Kantishna Experience" tour. The 13-hour adventure, which takes guests to the end of the drivable portion of the Denali Park Road at mile No. 92, will be available to reserve in 2027. (The road is currently closed.) Complimentary shuttle service to the Denali Visitors Center and the Denali Bus Depot (where you'll meet your tour) is available when you're staying in one of the cruise line's hotels, such as the Denali Princess Wilderness Lodge or the Holland America Denali Lodge. You can also book tours through the property's guest services desks, but it's advisable to book them in advance, as they often sell out. It's important to note that private vehicles are limited to the first 15 miles of Denali Park Road, which ends at Savage River. You'll need to book either a transit bus or a narrated tour bus to explore farther into the park. Ride the rapids in Denali with a white water rafting tour This 3 1/2-hour adventure on the Nenana River takes thrill-seekers on an 11-mile journey through white water rapids with views of Denali's Mount Healy and Sugarloaf Mountain in the distance. You can opt to hold on as an oar boat rider, making the tour accessible for almost anyone. More intrepid and active travelers (15 years of age and older) can paddle through the waves along with the guide. The minimum age for the tour is 12. There's also a weight limit of 265 pounds for Princess Cruise Line. The outfitter provides the appropriate gear, including a dry suit, a helmet, paddle river shoes and a life jacket. You can reserve the excursion in advance or through guest services at one of the wilderness lodges. Be sure to bring a waterproof case for your smartphone so you can take photos and videos during the wild ride. Expect to pay around $149 for the excursion. Take the drive of a lifetime along the Denali Highway This 135-mile stretch of gravel road was once the gateway to the park and was named the No. 2 "Drive of a Lifetime" by National Geographic Traveler. With the guided and narrated 4 1/2-hour "Denali Highway Jeep Excursion," you'll travel approximately 50 miles along the Denali Highway (100 miles round-trip) for unparalleled views and photo opportunities. The four-wheeling Jeep tour will take you past some of Alaska's most spectacular scenery, including vast glaciers, the snowcapped mountains of the Alaska Range, far-reaching vistas and, on a clear day, views of Denali's peak. You may also encounter some wildlife, so be sure to bring your binoculars (in addition to your camera). Expect to pay around $189 per adult and $119 for kids 12 and under. You must be 25 or older to drive. Fairbanks is one of the best places in the world to witness the magical (but sometimes elusive) northern lights. On a cool, clear evening, you may be able to see the light show dance across the night sky during aurora season, which falls between Aug. 21 and April 21. The Explore Fairbanks website has an Aurora Tracker that correlates data from three different sources to predict the chances of seeing the lights across six areas in and around Fairbanks, so you can check the probability of viewing the lights while you're in town. Cruise lines offer late-night to early morning tours (typically 10 p.m. to 3 a.m.) as optional excursions during aurora season, but you can also book an independent tour through a local provider. Some companies also offer photography tours, where you can learn how to capture natural phenomena. A top-rated excursion that you can book on your own is the 9-hour Northern Lights Tour from Fairbanks with Face the Outdoors. The small-group experience (maximum 10 guests) includes a pickup from your hotel where you'll travel to a private wilderness lodge for optimal aurora viewing. Here, you'll have a toasty warm indoor space with a fireplace, panoramic windows along with complimentary hot drinks and snacks. If necessary (due to weather), the guide may chase the northern lights by heated van to another location. In addition, tour-goers will receive photography assistance with cameras or smartphones and aurora photos from the experience. (Note that this tour is not wheelchair accessible.) Prices start at $359 per person. Take a flightseeing adventure over the Arctic Circle This bucket-list trip from Fairbanks crosses the Arctic Circle, which is approximately 140 air miles north of town. Once you've arrived, you'll be in the far north polar region, formally known as the "Land of the Midnight Sun." Holland America Line's approximately six-hour optional excursion across the Arctic Circle includes a flight over the Yukon River valley and the Brooks Range, landing just outside Alaska's Gates of the Arctic National Park & Preserve in Coldfoot. You'll also have 2 1/2 hours on land to visit the wilderness communities of Coldfoot and Wiseman and learn how the few residents who call this remote area home survive the winter with extreme temperatures that reach as low as minus 80 degrees Fahrenheit. A souvenir Arctic Circle Certificate is awarded at the end of the trip. The weight limit is 340 pounds. You can also reserve one of these tours independently with a local tour operator. Prices start at $729 per person, but vary based on the length of the excursion, departure time and season. Play a round of golf at the northernmost 18-hole golf course in the US You'll come home with another certificate saying you played at the northernmost golf course in the country after a round of golf at the Midnight Sun Golf Course in Fairbanks. This six-hour excursion (prices from $169 per person) is a true Alaska adventure, featuring a late-evening golf game between May and July (when the sun doesn't set, from approximately May 17 to July 27) on a rustic course underlain with permafrost.
