item.title: I Indulged in Rare, 135-Year-Old Wine at This Sonoma Resort
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
In Hotels With Great Taste, weâre pulling back the curtain for a peek at the âspecial sauceâ that hotels use to create memorable, meaningful culinary experiences for their guests. Look closely at the lodgings that make up Dawn Ranch and youâll notice theyâre actually a patchwork of historic structures in different shapes and sizes. Each building at the luxe 15-acre Russian River resort, which is nestled amongst the towering redwoods in the petite town of Guerneville, California, is linked to a different era of the propertyâs past. Built in 1905, it was originally Murphyâs Ranch, a getaway for well-to-do families that operated for seven decades. Later it served for more than 20 years as the pioneering gay resort Fifeâs. Today, itâs a refined wine country escape that exists at the crossroads of nature and high-end luxury. The hotel is situated in a floodway, which limits construction for safety purposes, so since 1993 the siteâs various owners havenât been able to build anew; renovating ad infinitum has proven to be just dandy though. In fact, this limitation turns out to be central to Dawn Ranchâs retro, summer camp-adjacent charm, which feels like a happy throwback even with its modernized facilities and amenities. Spectacularly refurbished in 2023, the current upscale iteration features 81 California-cool rooms, a tremendous spa, a fine-dining restaurant that may very well become impossible to book once word gets out, and a thoughtful, dynamic wine program that highlights some of the worldâs most unique bottles. When it comes to bunking, you have choices that span a hodgepodge of rustic-chic cabins, chalets, cottages, bungalows, and glamping tents. On the main campus, cabins are cozy and compact, while the cottages and chalets offer more space. Most include private outdoor decks, equally ideal for taking in a morning cuppa or an evening tipple. The bungalows are the roomiest accommodation, outfitted for families and large groups with two bedrooms, two baths, a full kitchen, and gas fireplaces. Across the street, the resortâs Grove campus offers more options, which range from snug single-room affairs to spacious two bedrooms. Theyâre all scattered amongst the tree-filled propertyâs sycamores and redwoods, so traipsing to your room feels like a walk in the forest. Inside, the aesthetic is a study in NorCal quiet luxury, with plenty of smooth blonde wood, layered textiles, and eclectic furniture pieces, plus Parachute linens and Le Labo bath goodies. More adventurous guests will appreciate the smartly furnished glamping tents, situated in Dawn Ranchâs 120-year-old apple tree orchard. The walls may be canvas, but the beds feature the same Bear hybrid mattresses as those in Dawn Ranchâs more conventional rooms. You will, however, have to share a bathhouseâalbeit an extremely nice oneâwith your fellower glampers. No matter where you sleep, make sure you lay eyes on the resortâs namesake, a 70-year-old pair of rare dawn redwoods located near the pool on the main campus. The Lodge at Dawn Ranch, which houses the hotelâs main dining, bar, and lounge areas, manages a laid-back vibe that nonetheless feels rarefied and celebratory, with plush mauve-colored banquettes and dim romantic lighting. But food is the real draw: Co-executive chefs (and husband-and-wife team) Ignacio âNachoâ Zuzulich and Juliana Thorpe center a nine-course, $155 tasting menu informed both by their respective Argentinian and Brazilian backgrounds and their experience cooking in lauded kitchens from Mugaritz in Spain to Napa Valleyâs Meadowood resort. A truncated version of the tasting menu is served at the bar for $90. Seasonal Golden State ingredients take top billing. On a recent visit, corn was a standout, taking the form of a delicate tostada set atop a fire-roasted corn custard. Festooned with the marigold-like flowering herb huacatay, it conveyed an impossibly large, flawless lobe of Santa Barbara uni. In the morning, donât skip breakfast at the Lodge, which is best taken on the sprawling outside deck. Soft scrambled eggs with avocado and furikake on homemade brioche are straightforward but deeply effective, while the cinnamon rolls glossed in cream cheese frosting are the perfect excuse to eat dessert before noon. When drinking, whether in the dining room or bar, vino is the move. This is wine country, after all. The handwritten âSommelierâs Notebookâ dispenses with formality, breaking wines into playful categories like âThe Wild Ones,â âExtrovert Whites,â and âQuiet Elegance.â Youâll have plenty of fun ordering by the bottle or glass; if youâre after just a taste, some offerings are available in one-ounce pours. But for the deep-pocketed, the $400 Decades Wine Pairing is a voyage through time and space, guiding you through wines bottled across generations. The offerings frequently shift, but this past summer, the oldest pour was an intensely molasses-forward D'Oliveiras Verdelho Madeira, first put under cork in 1891. With its decadent syrup-like texture and vibrant acidity, the Madeira made for a complex complement to the tasting menuâs show-stopping dessert course, which presented local peaches in three manners: a quenelle of peach sorbet; a crystal cupful of peach nectar; and a tart of roasted peach jam and white chocolate ganache, topped with intricately woven, paper-thin peach slivers and served alongside a peach sabayon. Best of all, returning to my cottage after dinner required only a brief, tipsy walk through the redwoods, the stars lighting my way.

item.title: This Bryce Canyon Hike Rivals the Grand Canyon’s Rim-to-Rim Trail—and No One’s on It
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine
Group of hikers trekking through Bryce Canyon National Park, Utah, with rugged red rock formations in view. (Photo: Alex Moliski) Bryce Canyon might be America’s most spectacular drive-through national park. Visitors pull into an overlook, admire a thousand orange hoodoos, snap a photo, and drive to the next viewpoint. It’s fast food for the eyes: beautiful, looks great on your feed, and over in minutes. But I wanted more than the Happy Meal. So I shouldered my pack at Bryce Point and headed down the Under-the-Rim Trail, leaving the overlooks and crowded dayhikes behind for an overnight adventure. What I found was another Bryce Canyon entirely, where the landscape becomes something you walk through rather than look down upon. I expected more of the same orange hoodoos that made Bryce famous. Instead, I wandered through pine forests, sandy hills, and open meadows. The towering formations hadn’t disappeared. They were just above me now, casting unfamiliar shadows across the landscape. Beneath the rim, Bryce felt less like a geological spectacle and more like a wilderness. Trailhead: Start: Bryce Point, End: Rainbow Point Distance: 23.60 miles (my GPS numbers) Elevation: 5,167 feet (my GPS numbers) Permits: Required for all overnight trips The first surprise came barely two miles in. The “Hat Shop” is a collection of odd hoodoos resembling people wearing oversized hats, with enormous boulders balanced on skinny pillars. Whoever named it deserves a raise. But don’t forget to turn around: You’ve already dropped almost a thousand feet below Bryce Point, and the view looking back is one most visitors will never see. That initial descent is deceiving. About four miles in, you’re at the bottom of the first big drop, but the trail is far from finished climbing. The remaining miles are full of what our backpacking group calls “PUDs,” or pointless ups and downs. Stunning, certainly, but brutal on the legs. Those PUDs led to an ongoing debate amongst our group: Which is harder, the Grand Canyon’s (currently closed) Rim-to-Rim or Bryce’s Under-the-Rim Trail? I’ve now hiked both, and the similarities are surprising. Both cover more than 20 miles, demand thousands of feet of elevation change, and reward you with spectacular Southwest scenery. Opinions are split, but I give the difficulty crown to Bryce. Those relentless ups and downs really add up, and so do the endless changing views. The Grand Canyon might be the undisputed king of desert backpacking, but I think Bryce deserves a place in the same conversation. With flooding, fire damage, and construction disrupting the Grand Canyon’s famous Rim-to-Rim route, this is another adventure worth considering just a few hours north. It’s not the Grand Canyon, and that’s exactly the point. My favorite stretch came between the Swamp Canyon and Whiteman Bench connecting trails. For roughly two miles, the trail passes through an old burn scar where the forest is slowly reclaiming the landscape. Normally, walking through burned trees feels somber. Here, fresh green growth fills the gaps, and the thinned forest opens up enormous views that the living trees once concealed. Swamp Canyon Butte and Mud Canyon Butte tower above you, with Bryce’s massive walls rising on your opposite side. Buttes look better from below, if you ask me. This is where you start feeling small—where the park’s big crowds become a distant memory, and the wilderness really creeps in. I thought about the Southern Paiute story of how the hoodoos were formed. “Legend People,” whom the trickster god Coyote turned to stone, were forever frozen in time. Looking up at those towering formations, it wasn’t hard to imagine those figures watching us pass. Bryce Canyon itself was named for Ebenezer Bryce, an early settler who reportedly described the rugged landscape as “a helluva place to lose a cow.” After navigating its maze of drainages and forests, I understood his frustration—though getting lost in the scenery was precisely why I’d come. Fortunately, getting an overnight permit is easier than finding Ebenezer’s missing livestock. When we arrived at the packed visitor center, the ranger perked up at the mention of backpacking, apparently excited to discuss something other than the Navajo Loop. They told us we were the only backpackers heading out that week. You can reserve permits on Recreation.gov up to three months ahead, with an in-person ranger check-in required before departure. Bear-resistant canisters are also required, and the park lends them out for free (yes, there are black bears in Bryce). The whole process is very easy, since the trail is still overshadowed by other “bucket list” hiking and backpacking routes in the area. Campsites are designated, and spacing makes planning important. Swamp Canyon and Natural Bridge are good options for breaking up the route, though neither guarantees equal mileage. You could make this a two-night trip and camp at both, but we were only permitted for a single night. At Swamp Canyon, we found flat tent pads and a designated cooking area. Water is the bigger headache. Unlike canyon hikes that follow a river, Under-the-Rim crosses long, usually dry washes that finger down from the tall wall. On our trip, the reliable stops were Yellow Creek early on and Iron Spring much closer to the finish. That meant carrying extra water across all those PUDs. Seasonal sources vary, so check with a ranger, treat everything you collect, and consider caching water at permitted trail junctions. Both Yellow Creek and Iron Spring dry up entirely by mid-summer. Timing is equally tricky. I hiked on April 27, hoping for green forests without the summer heat. I wish I’d waited another week for spring to wake up. Late spring and early fall offer appealing windows, but snow, freezing nights, and summer thunderstorms all deserve consideration. Bring layers, sun protection, and plenty of water. It was hot during the day and freezing at night. It made for the kinds of mornings where I really didn’t want to get out of my sleeping bag. Finally, remember that Under-the-Rim is a point-to-point hike from Bryce Point to Rainbow Point. The regular park shuttle doesn’t serve Rainbow Point, so arrange transportation ahead of time. We parked a car at both trailheads to make it easy. NPS offers other options for shuttling from Rainbow Point on its website. And here’s the funny part: Getting back means driving the same scenic road I’d spent the whole trip trying to escape. There I was, dusty and tired, sitting in national park traffic with everyone else, admiring those same orange hoodoos from the comfort of a car. Only now, I’d also seen them from below. On the trail, I was a backpacker. On the drive back, I was a tourist. And you know what? There’s nothing wrong with being both. Bryce is a damn beautiful place, no matter which angle you look at it from.

item.title: Royal Caribbean cruise ships ranked by size from biggest to smallest — the complete list
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Are you looking for the most activity-packed, megaresort-like Royal Caribbean cruise ships at sea? If so, you'll want to get on one of the biggest Royal Caribbean cruise ships. These ships are, by nature, the Royal Caribbean ships with the most pools, waterslides and other top-deck activities, as well as the most onboard restaurants, bars and showrooms. They have the biggest casinos and spas among ships in the Royal Caribbean fleet, as well as the largest number of cabins and suites — and the most variation in cabin and suite types. With room for more than 6,000 passengers, the biggest Royal Caribbean ships are truly massive resorts like the ones you'd find at landlocked destinations such as Orlando and Las Vegas. If you're in the "bigger is better" camp when it comes to a resort experience, these are the Royal Caribbean ships for you. Royal Caribbean doesn't only operate massive vessels, though. The Miami-based cruise giant also operates several relatively small ships that carry just 2,000 or 3,000 passengers and have a much more intimate feel. In some cases, these vessels are just half or one-third of the size of Royal Caribbean's biggest ships. These ships, notably, have far fewer top-deck activities and interior venues than the biggest Royal Caribbean cruise ships. The smallest Royal Caribbean cruise ships are best for vacationers who like a more intimate, less crowded resort experience. To ensure you end up on the right ship for you, it pays to study which Royal Caribbean ships are the biggest and which are the smallest before booking. Here is every Royal Caribbean ship currently in operation, ranked from biggest to smallest. Note: Ships are ranked based on gross registered tonnage — the measure of a ship's interior volume. Passenger numbers listed are based on double occupancy (two people per cabin). Royal Caribbean cruise ships, biggest to smallest What is the biggest Royal Caribbean ship? The three biggest Royal Caribbean cruise ships are Icon of the Seas, Star of the Seas and Legend of the Seas. All three are Icon Class ships measuring 248,663 gross tons, making them tied for the biggest ships in the Royal Caribbean fleet — and also the biggest cruise ships ever built by any line. They’re loaded with more bars, restaurants, theaters and top-deck attractions than you'll find on any other ship at sea. Icon of the Seas debuted in 2024, followed by Star of the Seas in 2025 and Legend of the Seas in 2026. item.title: Hike of the Week: Colorful Mushrooms, Not Leaves, Are the Main Attraction on This Fall Overnight
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine
Washington State hikers have made headlines this month for clogging up highways, parking areas, and trails in pursuit of Larch Madness—the fleeting time of year when deciduous conifers bedeck the alpine with their brilliant aureate needles. The fall colors are indeed stunning, but if you prefer not to hike nose-to-tail with hundreds of others, there are plenty of solitudinous trails worth visiting in October. Last weekend, I experienced the best of autumn in the PNW on this seldom-visited overnight route in the Mt. Baker Wilderness. The trail was alive with mushrooms, moss, and clear skies to backdrop glacier views from a subalpine camp—and my hiking partner and I had it all to ourselves. A washout on the dirt forest service road to the Elbow Lake and Ridley Creek trailheads means you’ll have to work a little harder to reach the trails, but it’s worth it for the solitude. A gently climbing 4-mile bike ride or walk on the dirt road from the closure to the trailhead follows leaf-lined gravel alongside the Middle Fork Nooksack River, making for as pleasant a roadwalk as you could ask for. The loop itself wends through a forest that’s exploding with fall activity: Moss lining the forest floor and dripping from the trees is turning a deep emerald with the beginning of the wet season. Massive fungi of all shapes and pigments are reaching their peak: chanterelle, bear’s head tooth, violet webcap, rusulla, king boletes, and more paint the forest with fall colors of their own, from deep violet and rust red to sunshine yellow and snowy white. The loop’s highpoint is Mazama Camp, which offers wide-open mountain views. The Park Butte fire lookout perches on the prominence above; we heard laughter from the lookout as we cooked dinner, but never saw another camper (Park Butte is a popular destination for dayhikers and campers, but most hikers reach it from the Park Butte trailhead on the other side of the ridge.) We watched the Easton and Squak glaciers on Mt. Baker’s looming slopes turn blush pink at sunset. To the west, the apricot-colored dunite crags of the Twin Sisters lent their own unique hues to the landscape. On the hike out, we craned our necks to take in enormous Alaska yellow cedar and western hemlock, then stopped for lunch on the peaceful and sun-drenched shores of Elbow Lake. Park at a pullout beside the road closure at milepost 7 on Middle Fork Nooksack Rd (FSR 38)—a Discover Pass is required for parking here. Bike or walk 3.7 miles up the dirt road to the Elbow Lake trailhead. Here, stash your bikes in the woods and continue walking the last 1.4-mile stretch up the road to the Ridley Creek trailhead. From the rocky shore of the Middle Fork Nocksack River, look for a newly-installed log crossing with a rope handrail, which offers solid footing. [Note: Two sturdy log crossings exist as of October 2026, but these tend to wash out seasonally.] Across the river, climb a series of steep switchbacks through mature forest. Once you’ve worked up a pleasant burn in your calves, bust out of the trees into subalpine meadows where water sources are abundant in fall. After just 3 miles of hiking from the trailhead (about 8 from your car), set up for the night at Mazama Camp, where you can choose between a log shelter or one of a few scenic tent sites. Optionally, take a 3-mile roundtrip, 950-foot detour up to the Park Butte lookout for views over Mt. Baker, the Twin Sisters, and into the North Cascades. Spend the night at Mazama Camp, then the next day complete the loop by following the Bell Pass Trail for 4.4 miles until it dumps into the Elbow Lake trail. At mile 13.5, enjoy a break on the slice of land between Elbow Lake and Lake Doreen (there are also campsites in the area) before busting out the final 3 miles to the Elbow Lake trailhead. Just before reconnecting with the road, look for another log crossing over the Middle Fork Nooksack: This one also features a handline, but the log hasn’t been leveled on top like the other—step carefully, especially in wet conditions. After crossing, rejoin the forest road and ride or walk back to the car. It’s clear this loop gets less traffic than others in the area; the path is overgrown in spots, and several blowdowns cross the upper section of the Elbow Lake Trail, but the way is mostly clear thanks to hard work by local crews and volunteers. The rugged nature of the trail makes it feel all the more remote and special.

item.title: These 3 amazing Princess tours of Alaska will get you deep into the wilderness
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
These 3 amazing Princess tours of Alaska will get you deep into the wilderness Looking to see a wide range of Alaska's most famous wilderness areas in a single trip? A "cruisetour" organized by Princess Cruises® could be the answer. The California-based cruise company has long been the leader in Alaska cruisetours, which pair a cruise along the state's southeastern coast with overland touring into its rugged interior. Princess is also known for longer cruisetour itineraries that cover many of Alaska's most celebrated destinations in a single, easy-to-arrange trip. Among the 28 Alaska cruisetour itineraries that Princess offers, more than any other company, for instance, are several epic options up to 17 nights in length covering not only Denali National Park and Glacier Bay National Park*, but also at least one and sometimes two additional major national parks. These extra parks include Kenai Fjords National Park, home to one of North America's most spectacular ice fields and glacier-carved fjords, and Wrangell-St. Elias National Park, the largest national park in the United States. Princess notably owns its own lodges and infrastructure at all these national park destinations — something no other tour company can say. Princess also owns its own fleet of glass-domed rail cars and motorcoaches for transportation between destinations. Here, a look at three of Princess's most ambitious cruisetours, each covering multiple national park visits. For a deeper dive into all 28 cruisetour itineraries, which range from 10 to 17 nights, see our related guide to Princess cruisetours in Alaska. 3 major national parks, including Kenai Fjords Tour name: 15-day Denali Escorted (tour code UB8) Denali National Park and Preserve is probably Alaska's most well-known national park, but don't overlook the lesser-visited Kenai Fjords National Park. South of Anchorage on Alaska's stunning Kenai Peninsula, the giant park (nearly as big as Rhode Island) is a major hub for outdoor pursuits and plays a big role in this Princess tour. Travelers will spend three nights at the Kenai Princess Wilderness Lodge®, allowing plenty of time to explore Kenai Fjords National Park and the surrounding area. Home to the massive Harding Icefield, one of the largest ice fields in the U.S. and numerous glacier-carved fjords, the park itself offers visitors the chance to see a glacier up close on foot, by boat, by kayak or by flightseeing tour. Visitors can spot wildlife like Steller sea lions, puffins, Dall's porpoises, American black bears, snowshoe hares, mountain goats and humpback whales. Other popular activities include world-famous salmon fishing and scenic float trips on the Kenai River, which flows 75 miles from Cooper Landing (where the Kenai Princess Wilderness Lodge is) to Cook Inlet. There are also hiking trails just outside the lodge. This tour pairs a three-night stay at the Kenai Princess Wilderness Lodge with a three-night stay at Princess-owned lodging in the Denali National Park area and a two-night stay in Fairbanks, Alaska. Princess combines this eight-day overland tour with a seven-night cruise along the Southeast Alaska coast for a total of 15 days. On the cruise portion of the trip, you will experience Glacier Bay National Park* and Preserve*, a third major national park. 3 major national parks, including Wrangell-St. Elias Tour name: 13-day Denali Escorted (tour code SB6) Quick, can you name the largest national park in the United States? If you said Yellowstone National Park or Grand Canyon National Park, you'd be off by a margin. The biggest national park in the United States by far is one you may not even know: Wrangell-St. Elias National Park and Preserve. It measures more than 20,000 square miles — about six and 10 times the size of Yellowstone and Grand Canyon, respectively. In south-central Alaska, the park is relatively unknown due to its remoteness. It draws fewer than 100,000 visitors a year. But seeing it, albeit briefly, is a key part of this unusual Princess tour. The 13-day trip includes an overnight stay at the Princess-owned Copper River Princess Wilderness Lodge, just down the road from the Wrangell-St. Elias National Park visitor center. The 85-room lodge offers spectacular views of the Wrangell Mountains, which are at the core of the park. It also overlooks one of Alaska's most famous human-made features: the Trans-Alaska Pipeline. For visitors, it serves as a base for hiking, salmon fishing, all-terrain-vehicle touring, rafting trips, jet boat tours, coastal kayaking, glacier-viewing boat tours and even a visit to the ghost town of Kennicott (a former mining camp). In addition to the overnight at Copper River Princess Wilderness Lodge, the land portion of this tour includes a four-night stay at Princess-owned lodging in the Denali National Park area and an overnight visit to Fairbanks, Alaska. This six-night overland tour is also paired with a seven-night cruise along the Southeast Alaska coast. As with the 15-day tour, the cruise will allow you to experience a third major national park, Glacier Bay National Park and Preserve.* Tour name: 17-day Denali Escorted (tour codes VB1 and VA1) If you want to go to both Kenai Fjords National Park and Wrangell-Saint Elias National Park on a single tour, this 17-day Princess journey is the one for you. This Alaska cruisetour — the longest Princess offers — includes two nights at Princess lodges at each of those parks, two nights each at its two Denali-area lodges (the Denali Princess Wilderness Lodge and Mount McKinley Princess Wilderness Lodge), and two nights at the Fairbanks Princess Riverside Lodge. For those counting, that's two full nights in each of Princess's five lodges in Alaska. As with all Princess cruisetours in Alaska, the 17-day trip also includes a seven-night cruise along the Southeast Alaska coast, with a visit to Glacier Bay National Park.* That means that you'll be able to see four of Alaska's eight national parks (Denali, Kenai Fjords, Wrangell-Saint Elias and Glacier Bay) in a single epic trip. The cruise also stops at Skagway, Alaska, a historic gold rush town, a significant portion of which falls within Klondike gold rush National Historical Park. That brings the total to five national park sites on the voyage. You can take this vacation two ways: either go on the overland tour first or the cruise portion. If you choose the cruise portion first, you will experience one slight variation. Your ship will visit the College Fjord glacier area instead of Hubbard Glacier (both are great for glacier viewing). Princess Cruises is known for long Alaska tours that combine cruise and overland travel to reach some of the state's most celebrated wilderness destinations. If you're looking for a single trip that can get you to iconic Alaska destinations like Denali National Park, Glacier Bay National Park*, Kenai Fjords National Park and Wrangell-St. Elias National Park, a Princess cruisetour is one of the strongest options available. *Princess Cruises is an authorized concessioner of Glacier Bay National Park. Planning a cruise? Start with these stories: Yes. All three tours mentioned in this guide include meals during their land portions. To ensure you get the exact departure date you want for these tours, it's a good idea to book 10 to 12 months in advance. There are relatively few spots on each of these tours, so booking far in advance ensures you will have first pick of departure dates and specific cabin categories and cabins for the cruise portion of the trip. You are not required to book flights through Princess and can book your own flights to and from the starting and ending points for these tours. If booking independently, make sure to adhere to Princess's recommended arrival and departure times. At TPG, we always recommend that travelers fly to any cruise or cruisetour a day before the scheduled start of the trip so that they don't miss the trip in the event of a flight delay. The season for Alaska cruisetours is very short, lasting from May to September, so those are the only months when you can do any of these three tours. Among these months, June and July offer the longest daylight hours (with up to 18 hours of sunlight for sightseeing), while July and August are the peak months for viewing whales and bears. May and September, which are the "shoulder season" months at the start and end of the Alaska cruise season, often are less crowded in Alaskan ports and can bring somewhat lower fares.

item.title: A Rare Super El Niño Is on the Way. Here Is Where Snow Will Fall.
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine
You’ve probably heard about the weather phenomenon called Super El Niño, which climate scientists predict will impact winter weather. And if you’re a skier, this year’s Super El Niño could bring some pretty good news, with parts of the American West expected to get more snow than usual. According to the 2026-27 winter forecast by AccuWeather, a U.S. weather prediction service, parts of the Sierra Nevada, Great Basin, Wasatch Range, and Central Rockies could see above-average snowfall this season, with parts of the Southern Rockies also expected to get more snow than last winter (which, let’s be real, wouldn’t really be hard to do). Meanwhile, much of the Northeast, Midwest, and Pacific Northwest might not be so lucky. AccuWeather’s lead long-range forecaster Paul Pastelok told Outside that California, Utah, and Colorado should all have favorable skiing conditions this winter, though California could experience more frequent storms and greater travel disruptions. “The West definitely looks like a better bet for skiers hoping to find consistently good snow conditions this winter, largely because of how strong this El Niño is,” Pastelok said. Pastelok told Outside that the term Super El Niño isn’t an official scientific classification. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) categorizes El Niño events as weak, moderate, strong or very strong, depending on how much warmer than normal the tropical Pacific Ocean becomes. “Super” is simply a weatherperson’s way of saying “very strong.” And this year’s El Niño could be one for the record books. Every few years, waters in the central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean become unusually warm. That extra heat changes where air rises, clouds form and rain falls, which can alter weather patterns thousands of miles away. One of the biggest changes involves the jet stream, a band of fast-moving winds high in the atmosphere that acts a bit like a highway for storms. During an El Niño winter, that highway typically shifts farther south, steering more storms and precipitation toward California and the southern United States. Meanwhile, northern states tend to experience warmer, drier conditions. What makes this year’s El Niño super is the strength of the warming. In its October 8 outlook, NOAA estimated an 83 percent chance that this El Niño would surpass the strength of every event in its historical record dating back to 1950 during the October-to-December period. “The stronger the El Niño gets, the more confident we feel that typical El Niño conditions will occur,” Pastelok told Outside. Here’s where AccuWeather expects the snow to fall, and what that means for skiers. California could see repeated bouts of heavy mountain snow as a series of Pacific storms, including atmospheric rivers, moves inland. Pastelok expects several atmospheric rivers to arrive during the winter, specifically during the middle and latter parts of the season. Those storms could deliver feet of snow in the mountains, although heavy precipitation could also create flooding and landslide risks at lower elevations. “There may be more snow in California,” Pastelok said, comparing the state’s outlook with Utah and Colorado. “But the downside for California is that it could be much stormier, making travel to ski resorts more difficult than in Utah or Colorado.” Utah’s Wasatch Range is also expected to benefit from an active southern storm track, with above-average snowfall possible across the region. AccuWeather predicts Salt Lake City will receive between 50 and 65 inches of snow this winter, compared with just 3.7 inches last season, the city’s least snowy winter on record. Those figures represent snowfall in the city rather than the nearby mountains, where accumulations are substantially greater. That’s good news for skiers hoping to carve turns at Park City, Snowbird, Alta, and the region’s other world-famous resorts. Colorado and the Central and Southern Rockies could also see a significant improvement over last winter. AccuWeather expects an early start to the snow season across the region, with additional storms arriving as winter progresses. By February, the Four Corners region is forecast to experience cooler-than-average temperatures and above-average precipitation, conditions that could support additional mountain snowfall. Pastelok said Colorado might not receive as much snow as California this winter, but should still experience good skiing conditions. The Great Basin, which stretches across Nevada and portions of neighboring states, is another region where AccuWeather expects above-average snowfall. The forecast favors an early start to the snow season across the region, although AccuWeather has not provided specific seasonal accumulation estimates for individual mountain areas. The snow outlook is less promising across much of the Pacific Northwest and Northern Rockies, where periods of snowfall could be interrupted by extended dry stretches. In the Northeast, warmer temperatures and below-average snowfall could create particularly difficult conditions for lower-elevation ski areas. Pastelok said smaller ski areas could struggle to maintain adequate snow coverage as repeated warm spells bring rain and ice. “When people hear that, they assume it’s going to be a bad ski season,” Pastelok said. “And for many smaller, lower-elevation ski areas, that’s probably true. Warmer temperatures, rain and ice are going to make it difficult to keep snow on the slopes.” But higher-elevation resorts in northern Vermont and New Hampshire could fare better, and the region may still experience significant snowstorms in late January or February. He added that three previous Super El Niño winters brought major snowstorms to the Northeast in late January or early February, potentially offering skiers some relief after an otherwise disappointing season. “The season could start out poorly, but a big snowstorm in late January or February could still give skiers a good weekend on the slopes,” he said. Before booking a weeklong ski vacation based on the forecast, there’s one thing worth keeping in mind, Pastelok said. Seasonal snowfall predictions are better at identifying broad weather patterns than predicting conditions at a particular mountain on a particular date. Pastelok said long-range forecasters use historical weather patterns and current atmospheric conditions to identify which regions are most likely to experience active storm periods. But even an exceptionally strong El Niño can throw forecasters a curveball. For example, Pastelok said that during the powerful El Niño of 2015-16, the jet stream shifted farther north than expected, leaving Southern California and the Four Corners region, including Colorado, with less snow than forecasters had anticipated. And even when the storms do arrive, more precipitation doesn’t necessarily mean more snow. If temperatures are warm enough, it could fall as rain instead. AccuWeather plans to update its winter forecast in mid-November, Pastelok said. While a seasonal forecast might help skiers decide which part of the country to visit, figuring out exactly when to book that trip is another matter. “If you’re asking me, should I go on a snow trip on February 2 because we’re going to get a lot of snow right before that?” Pastelok said. “That’s hard for me to tell you right now.”

item.title: United extends new Wi-Fi status match aimed at Delta: Who's eligible to be Premier?
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
United Airlines has extended its “Switch To Better Wi-Fi” status-match offer through Oct. 22. The match had been set to end Oct. 15. See the original story below for all the details. The gloves are off in the battle for frequent flyer loyalty. United Airlines this week rolled out a new status match offer targeting the elite customers of rivals Delta Air Lines and American Airlines. Status match offers are nothing new. United already had its standard offer in place, allowing elite members of other big carriers to request that United match their existing status. But it’s United’s “Switch To Better Wi-Fi” offer that’s drawing attention across both mainstream media and aviation blogs thanks to its particularly pointed message at rival Delta. United is in the process of equipping its fleet with Starlink Wi-Fi, widely acknowledged as the fastest and most reliable inflight internet service provider today. Delta is taking a different track, instead choosing Amazon’s Leo service – so far unproven for in-flight capabilities – on a rollout that will lag United’s. American, which also plans to install Starlink beginning next year, also jumped into the fray — though only to promote its standard status match. But it’s what prompted United to take aim at Delta that’s generating publicity. United’s new status match offer came after comments Delta CEO Ed Bastian reportedly made to employees about Delta’s decision not to use Starlink were leaked. Included in those comments was commentary on perceived difficulties working with Starlink founder Elon Musk. That set off a firestorm of online chatter, with some Delta frequent flyers lamenting that United was going with a quicker rollout of a Wi-Fi product they perceived to be better. Both United and American opportunistically used the kerfuffle as a way to promote their existing status matches.
But then United went further, launching a new and separate status match offer aimed at Delta — though it also included American in the match opportunity. “Don’t keep buffering: switch to United and get the fastest Wi-Fi in the sky,” the airline said. “This is war, airline style,” airline analyst Henry Harteveldt told CNBC. “It’s very rare for an airline to be as blatant as United is being" in its pitch against its main rivals. Regardless of where one stands in the back-and-forth over Starlink and Musk, there’s a clear opportunity here for frequent flyers to try out the elite benefits of United's MileagePlus program. Here’s what you need to know about United’s match offers, including the carrier's newest internet-inspired one that United calls “our most flexible and straightforward status match yet.” ‘Switch To Better Wi-Fi’ status match details This offer is open to customers with elite status on Delta or American (U.S. residents only). Typically, United allows a customer to request a status match only once every three years, but it is waiving that requirement for the Wi-Fi match. (United’s full terms and conditions are here.) If approved, United will match applicants to a United Premier status tier that corresponds with the current status a customer has earned on either Delta or American. Approved applicants will keep that status with United for 90 days, with the opportunity to extend it into January 2028 by hitting spending thresholds on qualifying flight purchases with United. The thresholds vary by status level. Additional match offers are also available for the invitation-only status levels for Delta (Delta 360) and American (Concierge Key). The Wi-Fi offer also differs from United's standard match. It's open to loyalists from a wider variety of airlines. With that offer, customers typically have 120 days to complete a challenge conferring full-year status, though those challenges consist of a combination of "Premier Qualifying Dollars" (PQDs) and "Premier Qualifying Flights" (PQFs) that United typically uses to determine status. United's Wi-Fi match will offer AA and Delta elites a simpler path to elite status with lower spending required. But that status match has a much shorter calendar in which to complete the challenge required to earn full-year benefits. As with the Wi-Fi match, additional offers are also available for the invitation-only status levels for Delta (Delta 360) and American (Concierge Key). This back-and-forth over airline Wi-Fi and status comes as carriers are increasingly leaning on free Wi-Fi as a perk for loyalty members. Delta has rolled our free connectivity for its SkyMiles members to a majority of its fleet, though the service is generally viewed as less fast than what Starlink offers. Its current Wi-Fi provider, Viasat, recently activated a new satellite that the company said will significantly improve bandwidth as Delta awaits Amazon Leo installations in the coming years. American also has plans to add Starlink to about 500 of its narrowbody planes, but — so far — has not detailed plans to expand the service to more of its fleet. Related reading:

item.title: Nara Smith Regrets Trying to Make Twizzlers
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
Nara Smithâs internet persona is built on a specific kind of perfection: extravagant gowns, immaculate kitchens, and from-scratch recipes that make artisanal homemade cereal feel entirely reasonable. A true modern renaissance woman, she seamlessly balances cooking, influencing, and motherhood, and is even set to star alongside Charlize Theron and Demi Moore in the upcoming thriller Tyrant, a film delving into NYCâs elite fine dining scene. Her new book, Homemade, balances her campy approach to cookingâthe cover features Smith in a dress that doubles as a tableâwith recipes for homemade cinnamon toast squares alongside more practical, kid-friendly dishes like pork schnitzel and Coconut Cassava Waffles. In person, sheâs far less precious and much funnier. During Smithâs visit to the Bon AppÃ©tit Test Kitchen, her relentless pace was on full display. When I ran down a couple of floors to return a pen her producer had left behind, I found her completely transformed, glam fully retouched, already posing for her next shoot for Vanity Fair. We spoke to Smith about the kitchen slippers hiding beneath her camera frame, the failed homemade Twizzlers that still haunt her, the sudden onset of her egg ick, and the oddly specific way her dad taught her to cut pancakes into tiny squares. Whatâs the first thing people get wrong about you? People think Iâm wearing heels. Iâm actually wearing slippers. Iâm very tall, and if I wear heels the counter is too low and nothing looks proportionate. Also, Iâm standing all day and my lower back would never forgive me. So itâs always a really good cushioned house slipper. Comfort first. You spend so much time making food on camera. Are there recipes that feel especially personal to you? These German pancakes. My dad made them before school when I was growing up. Heâd always make the first one before he woke us up because the first pancake is always bad. When I was writing the recipe for my cookbook, I asked him for measurements, and he was like, âA little bit of this, a little bit of that, maybe two, maybe three eggs.â That's not exactly cookbook language. Your cookbook is full of from-scratch recipes. Is there anything youâd never make yourself? Never say never. I tried making Twizzlers once, and they were terrible. Absolutely terrible. I still think about trying again because I love a challenge, but candy is one of those things that can really humble you. Whatâs been your biggest kitchen disaster? The Twizzlers were bad, but sourdough was probably worse. My first few attempts were a complete mess. The funny thing is I often make recipes for the first time on camera, so if something goes wrong, everyone gets to watch it happen in real time. The Test Kitchen wanted to know: Whatâs your favorite way to eat eggs? This is controversial because I have 20 chickens, but I got the egg ick while I was pregnant, and it never fully went away. If Iâm eating eggs, I want a fried egg with crispy edges and a runny yolk on top of fried rice. Just donât give it to me first thing in the morning. You garden too. Howâs that going? Honestly? My garden is dying. The zucchini is struggling. The cucumbers are gone. All my lettuce died. Between the heat and the rain, everything has kind of given up. Itâs my first year, though, so Iâm trying to be kind to myself. Next year will be better. Whatâs the most specific food habit you have? I cut these pancakes into tiny squares. My dad used to do it for me, and now itâs the only way I like eating them. I put applesauce on top, dust them with powdered sugar, cut them into little squares, and eat them one by one. Everyone else in my family thinks itâs weird. What's one cooking tip you swear by? Weigh your ingredients. Especially flour. A cup of flour means something different to everyone. Good ingredients matter, too, but if youâre baking, a scale will save you a lot of heartbreak.

item.title: Why Red Bull Got Into the Ski Business—And Teamed Up with an Austrian Racing Legend to Do It
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine
Plenty of skiers are gear-obsessed, but Marcel Hirscher is in a league of his own. Over the course of his 15-year racing career, the legendary Austrian skier and founder of VAN DEER-Red Bull Sports would drive his coaches and teammates crazy with constant chatter about tech specs and modifications. Maybe not the guy you want to challenge in gear trivia, but definitely the guy you want designing your skis. Which is why he’s the first person to convince Red Bull to co-own a ski brand. Born in Salzburg and raised in the Austrian Alps, Hischer made his World Cup debut in March 2007 and found himself catapulted into the limelight. In 2008, he bagged his first World Cup podium, and in 2009, his first win. Over the next 10 years, he became the winningest Austrian ski racer of all time, turning heads with masterful racing strategy and unparalleled technique. Credit those skills to his uncompromising perfectionism, a characteristic that drove him to 67 World Cup wins, two Olympic gold medals, and eight consecutive overall World Cup titles. And when he retired from ski racing in 2019, it’s what drove him to start manufacturing his own skis. Hirscher has always been a tinkerer by nature—maddeningly meticulous and chronically detail-oriented. Red Bull already knew that after a decade of working with him as a sponsor and supporter. So, when Hirscher said he was launching his own company in 2021, their ears perked up. Hischer called his brand VAN DEER, a name that plays up his half-Dutch heritage and winks at the fact that hirsch is German for “deer.” The goal was to give the brand some racing pedigree without directly naming it after a pro. After all, Hirscher never set out to make skis just for the elite. Hirscher’s overarching philosophy is that all skiers are equal. It doesn’t matter if you’re a bunny-hill newbie, a weekend warrior, or a champion racer. Everyone can benefit from a ski that fits, and everyone can access the sublime sense of flow and rhythm that only skiing can offer. “Nothing feels quite like a perfectly carved turn,” Hirscher says. “When a ski truly fits its skier, you feel it through a certain naturalness of movement.” He’s honed his sensitivity to that feeling through decades of racing. Now, he’s applying that fine-tuned sensibility to ski design. “For a ski racer, skiing is a constant search for hundredths of a second, where even a tiny change in edge angle or flex can make a huge difference,” says Hirscher. “The real challenge is transferring that knowledge from the racecourse to everyday skiers in a way that makes them better.” That process requires converting raw data and physics into the unquantifiable feeling of human movement. That’s the alchemy Hirscher lives for. He spent the first months of his new project immersed in the all-consuming process of design. Then Red Bull stopped by. After such a longstanding partnership, maybe it’s no wonder that Hirscher and Red Bull had developed a strikingly similar vision for the future of alpine skiing. Regardless, a collab was an easy yes. Red Bull got a peek at what Hirscher was doing, liked what they saw, and came on as a partner in 2022. The result: VAN DEER-Red Bull Sports. Since then, the Alps-based brand has become a beacon of Austrian heritage. The skis are sleek, classic, and no-nonsense. Their craftsmanship is decidedly traditional, but the high-tech materials and rigorous testing are as modern as it gets. The skis get put through their paces on mountains all over the world—including on World Cup courses where they’ve already earned gold medals and dozens of podium finishes. Hirscher even wore them himself when he returned to racing for the 2024/25 season. Better yet, the athletes who ride those skis deliver their feedback to VAN DEER-Red Bull Sports, a tight-knit partnership that continues to drive the pace of innovation. Two of those skis—the FREERIDE SERIES, which is exactly what it sounds like, and the H-POWER SERIES, which is designed for all-day skiing in any terrain—bring Hirscher’s profound knowledge and racing heritage to skiers across a wide range of skill levels. The new launches are also designed to complement the brand’s four existing lines: the PRO SERIES, RACE SERIES, JUNIOR PRO SERIES, and TOURING SERIES. “My mission is to make the feeling I have while skiing accessible to others,” Hirscher says. “With us, there is no racing privilege when it comes to material quality—we build skis with World Cup quality, adapted for free skiing.” Because while World Cup racing will always have a special place in Hirscher’s heart, his primary mission is to help up-and-coming skiers accelerate their mastery of the sport he loves. The goal isn’t only to help that new generation win more medals. It’s to help them fall in love with skiing—with each drop, each pole-plant, each turn—exactly in the same way he did. At VAN DEER-Red Bull Sports, founded in the Austrian Alps by ski legend Marcel Hirscher, we do things differently. We believe in the power of “new” and a no-compromise approach to skiing and equipment. Together with Red Bull, we combine racing expertise with innovation to create world-class skis for a new generation.
